title: Slavoj Žižek
keyWorks: Welcome to the Desert of the Real (2002)
summary: Slavoj Žižek is a Slovenian philosopher who brings together Hegel's philosophy, Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis and the analysis of popular culture. He is known for paradoxical turns of thought, jokes and readings of films. His central theme is ideology: not false ideas in our heads, but the way we live and act even when we "understand everything".
onEmotions: Following Lacan, Žižek holds that our desires and feelings never fully belong to us: we desire through others, through language and shared fantasies. A feeling, for him, is not simply an inner state but the place where our expectations collide with what Lacan called "the Real" — whatever does not fit into our familiar picture of the world. Žižek is suspicious of the culture of obligatory happiness and self-improvement: he calls it the injunction "Enjoy!", which brings more guilt than pleasure. His view is often uncomfortable, but it frees you: you don't need to be whole, and nobody is holding a final answer in reserve.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a heavy feeling, but an understandable one, and you don't have to get rid of it at any cost. Žižek, following Lacan, offers an unexpected angle: anxiety arises not when we lack something, but when the lack itself disappears — when what we desire, or other people's expectations, come too close and leave us no room. Lacan said that anxiety, unlike vague unease, does have an object — we just can't see it. From this point of view, your anxiety is not meaningless noise but a signal: something in your life has come right up against you, and you need a little distance. Žižek would remind you that you don't have to know and control everything. Sometimes relief comes when you admit that lack and uncertainty are a normal part of life.
anxiety.practice: Ask yourself: what or who has come "too close" to me right now — whose expectation, which question, what desire?

fear.text: Fear is an ancient protective reaction, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek would draw attention to how fear is used in today's world. In Violence he writes that many social forces now rely on fear — of strangers, of catastrophes, of change — because fear easily unites and controls. From this angle, one could say that some of what we fear has been suggested to us from outside, and it helps to tell your own fear apart from what the culture invites you to be afraid of. Žižek would also remind you that fear often hides a desire: we fear what at the same time attracts us. This view doesn't cancel the fear, but it makes it more understandable — and therefore a little smaller.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: is this fear my own, or did I "pick it up" from the people around me, the news, my feed?

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and it doesn't need to be hurriedly turned into positivity. Žižek likes to show how the culture of obligatory happiness makes sadness almost forbidden: we are urged to rejoice, to grow, to enjoy life. He calls this the command of the superego — the inner overseer who no longer says "you mustn't" but "enjoy!". When enjoyment becomes a duty, sadness looks like failure. From Žižek's point of view, one could say that your sadness is a refusal to take part in this show of cheerfulness, and there is honesty in it. It shows that something in your life doesn't fit the smooth picture. Letting yourself be sad means ceasing to obey an impossible order to be happy.
sadness.practice: Give yourself five minutes of sadness without trying to "fix" it. Notice whether this permission makes things even a little easier.

grief.text: Grief is a deep experience of loss, and it keeps to no timetable. Žižek often turns to Freud's distinction between mourning and melancholia. In mourning a person gradually lets go of what was lost; in melancholia they keep holding on to it. But Žižek, unlike many, sees in melancholia not only an illness: there is fidelity in it, a refusal to betray what was precious. From this point of view, one could say: if you can't "just let go", that isn't necessarily a mistake. Perhaps your grief is keeping something you are not ready to lose a second time. The way forward is not to forget, but to find a form of memory in which what you lost goes on living without taking the present away from you.
grief.practice: Think about it: what in what you lost do you want to keep forever — and how can that "something" live in your life now?

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and the fact that you feel it speaks of a deep need for connection. Žižek might offer an unexpected but comforting thought. Following Lacan, he repeats that "the big Other does not exist". The "big Other" is an imagined authority that sees everything, understands everything and guarantees meaning: God, society, public opinion. We often feel lonely because it seems that everyone else is connected to this authority and we are not. But for Žižek it doesn't exist for anyone: every person is in some way not fully understood and not fully fitted into the world. From this angle, your loneliness is not an exception but a shared human condition. And paradoxically, you can find kinship with others in that.
loneliness.practice: Imagine that the person who seems to you the most "fitted in" and self-assured also sometimes feels misunderstood. What changes?

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling: it tells you that something has truly touched a nerve. In Violence, Žižek distinguishes visible, "subjective" violence — outbursts, conflicts — from invisible, "objective" violence built into the very system of relations. Anger often reacts to the first, although the cause lies in the second. His advice may seem strange: don't act right away; stop and think. He believes that a hasty reaction often just reproduces the very thing we are angry about. From this point of view, your anger doesn't have to turn into action immediately. You can keep it as the energy of understanding: work out what exactly hurt you and where the real source of the problem lies. Then anger becomes not a flare-up but clarity.
anger.practice: Before you act, write down: what am I angry about "on the surface" — and what might lie deeper behind it?

shame.text: Shame is an agonizing feeling, and you deserve gentleness towards yourself within it. Žižek, following Lacan, would explain shame through the gaze — more precisely, through the imagined gaze of the "big Other", which seems to see right through us and judge us. We feel ashamed not so much before real people as before this imagined judge. But, as Žižek keeps repeating, the big Other does not exist: there is no all-seeing authority that passes a final verdict. From this angle, your shame rests on a court that doesn't actually exist. Žižek often quotes Beckett: failure is not the end but part of the way. You can allow yourself to be imperfect and carry on — without an all-seeing judge over your head.
shame.practice: Picture the one you feel ashamed before. Ask: is this a real person — or an imagined all-seeing judge?

quote.text: Ever tried. Ever failed. No matter. Try again. Fail again. Fail better.
quote.author: Samuel Beckett
quote.source: Worstward Ho (Žižek often quotes these lines)

guilt.text: Guilt speaks of your capacity for responsibility, and that is valuable. But Žižek, drawing on Freud, points to a paradox: the superego, the inner overseer, is built so that the more we obey it, the guiltier we feel. Its demands are impossible to meet by definition. Today, according to Žižek, the superego demands not strictness but enjoyment and self-realization: "be happy, be successful, grow!". And we feel guilty for failing at that too. From this point of view, one could say: if your guilt is endless, it may come not from a real wrongdoing but from an insatiable inner voice. You can hear it without having to obey it. Real responsibility is concrete; endless guilt is not.
guilt.practice: Ask yourself: if I put right what I feel guilty about, will the guilt go away? Or will the inner voice immediately find a new reason?

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but thoroughly human feeling, and admitting to it already takes courage. Žižek, following Lacan, holds that desire as such works through others: "desire is the desire of the Other". We want what others want, and what makes others desirable. So envy is not a random vice but the flip side of the very mechanism of desire. Žižek also writes about the fantasy of "stolen enjoyment": it seems to us that others enjoy life more fully than we do, as if they possessed a secret we have been deprived of. From this angle, your envy says more about a fantasy than about reality. You can acknowledge that nobody has complete enjoyment — and that takes the edge off the comparison.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: what do I imagine this person enjoys more than I do? And how much do I actually know about it?

emptiness.text: A sense of emptiness is hard, and it deserves attention rather than reproach. Žižek would offer an unexpected view. For him, as for Hegel, the human subject is not a full, whole thing but, at its core, a gap, a void, negativity. Hegel called this "the night of the world". Žižek sees this void not as a defect but as a source of freedom: precisely because we never fully coincide with any single role, we can change and create something new. From this point of view, one could say that the emptiness you feel doesn't necessarily mean something is wrong with you. Perhaps it lays bare what has always been at the core of a human being — a space from which something not yet known can emerge.
emptiness.practice: Instead of filling the emptiness, stay in it for a minute and ask: if this were not an absence but an open space, what might appear here?

confusion.text: Confusion is an honest response to a complicated world, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Žižek might even say it is the beginning of thinking. He shows how ideology works not through false ideas but through what seems obvious and natural. We often "know" how the world works, but that knowledge is just a familiar frame. When the frame cracks, confusion appears. For Žižek, this is a valuable moment: you can see that the obvious isn't obvious at all. He notes that sometimes we feel free only because we lack the words to describe our unfreedom. From this angle, confusion is a chance to find those words. There's no need to rush to an answer: a good question is worth more than a quick solution.
confusion.practice: Write down something that until recently seemed obvious to you but no longer does. What question grows out of it?

quote.text: We "feel free" because we lack the very language to articulate our unfreedom.
quote.author: Slavoj Žižek
quote.source: Welcome to the Desert of the Real

fatigue.text: Your tiredness is real, and it is not a sign of weakness. Žižek could help you see one of its causes. He describes a phenomenon that, after Octave Mannoni, he calls "fetishistic disavowal": "I know very well, but all the same…". We know very well that the endless race for success and self-improvement wears us out, but all the same we keep taking part in it, as if we didn't know. For Žižek, this is exactly how ideology works: not through ignorance, but through acting against what we know. From this point of view, your tiredness is the moment when the body stops pretending not to know. It is not defeat but a kind of honesty. You can allow yourself to admit what you have long known — and rest without excuses.
fatigue.practice: Finish the sentence: "I know very well that…, but all the same…". What do you keep doing against your own knowledge?

quote.text: They know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it.
quote.author: Slavoj Žižek

boredom.text: Boredom can be unpleasant, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek would perhaps explain it with humour. He likes to list the products of our time — coffee without caffeine, beer without alcohol, sweets without sugar — and sees in them a symbol of a culture in which everything has had its "dangerous" substance removed. We want experiences, but without risk; relationships, but without upheaval. From this angle, one could say that boredom is the natural result of a "decaf" life, where everything is safe but there is no real intensity. Your boredom may be a healthy signal: you are missing something real, something able to touch you and change you. It is not a complaint but a longing for the real, and it deserves attention.
boredom.practice: Ask yourself: where in my life is there something "decaf" — safe but bland? And what real thing would I like instead?

joy.text: Joy is a precious feeling, and you don't need to justify it. Žižek could help you tell genuine joy apart from obligatory enjoyment. Lacan used the word jouissance — an "enjoyment" that contains something excessive, even painful. Contemporary culture, according to Žižek, orders us to enjoy, and that turns pleasure into work. But real joy comes unexpectedly — as a gift, not as a completed task. Žižek himself prizes humour and absurdity: in a good joke there is a joy that arises from a gap, from an unexpected twist. From this point of view, one could say that you don't need to "do" joy correctly or hold on to it. It's enough simply to notice it — with laughter and gratitude for its chance nature.
joy.practice: Recall what made you smile or laugh unexpectedly today. Stay with that memory for a minute.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest human experiences. Žižek speaks about love paradoxically. Love, in his view, is not choosing the best option from a list of qualities but a fall: we love a person not for their merits, but together with their imperfections, and even through them. He remarks with irony that love is in a sense "unjust": it singles out one person from everyone and places them above the rest without any rational ground. Žižek also sees love as an event — something that breaks the habitual course of life. From this angle, your tenderness is neither weakness nor illusion, but a rare moment when you step beyond calculation. You can accept it with all its imperfect, unreasonable strength.
love.practice: Name one "imperfect" trait of someone you love that, for some reason, is dearer to you than any virtue.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that connects you with the world and with other people. Žižek didn't write about it specifically, but from the standpoint of his thought something interesting can be said. If, as he repeats after Lacan, "the big Other does not exist" and nobody guarantees us meaning or good fortune, then everything good in life is not an owed reward but a chance that might never have happened. That makes gratitude deeper: you are grateful not to a system that "owes" you something, but to a fragile coincidence of circumstances and to particular people. This view removes the expectation that the world is obliged to be fair, and lets you be surprised by the good. Gratitude becomes not a duty but wonder.
gratitude.practice: Name one good thing in your life that might very well not have been there. What is it like to realize how much it depended on chance?

hope.text: Hope is an important feeling, and it's good that you have it. Žižek's relation to hope is complicated. In The Courage of Hopelessness, following Giorgio Agamben, he criticizes easy, soothing hope — the kind that tells you to wait as if everything will sort itself out. But his conclusion is not gloomy: giving up false guarantees opens a space for real action. When we stop waiting for someone to come and fix everything, we gain the possibility of starting change ourselves. From this point of view, one could say that your hope grows stronger when it doesn't rest on illusions. It may sound not like "everything will definitely be fine" but like "I don't know how it will turn out, but I can take my own small step".
hope.practice: Rephrase your hope from "may … happen" to "I can do …". What is the small step in this new sentence?

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm, aching feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "objet a" — the object-cause of desire, which we experience as lost even though we never possessed it in full. The loss itself creates its value. From this point of view, one could say that the past you miss glows partly because it is gone — and memory tints it in colours that may not have been there at the time. That doesn't make your nostalgia false. On the contrary, it shows what you truly desire. Žižek would suggest asking: what exactly in the past is dear to you? Perhaps it can be found not only in memory but in the present too.
nostalgia.practice: Ask yourself: what am I really missing — a place and a time, or the feeling I had then? Where might that feeling be met now?

craving.text: A sharp "I want it right now" can be very strong, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek, following Lacan, would offer an unusual view. The thing you want — a cigarette, a glass, your phone — only temporarily occupies the place of what Lacan called the "objet a", the elusive cause of desire. That is why, having got what we wanted, we so often feel: "that's not it". Žižek liked the example of Coca-Cola: the more you drink, the thirstier you get. From this angle, one could say that a craving promises a fullness no thing can give — and the problem is not your weakness but the very nature of desire. Knowing this doesn't cancel the wave, but it changes how you relate to it: you have every right not to believe its promise. The wave rises and falls even if you don't feed it.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, ask: "What exactly is it promising me — calm, joy, oblivion?" Write that word down and watch how the wave changes.

addiction.text: If your life has long revolved around something that is hard to get out of, that is hard, and it is not a moral failure. Žižek, drawing on Lacan, distinguishes desire from drive. Desire seeks an object and is always disappointed; drive, by contrast, finds satisfaction in the circuit itself, in repetition. Lacan called this peculiar, almost painful pleasure jouissance. From this point of view, one could say that an addiction holds on not because the substance or habit is so very pleasant, but because the repeating circuit itself has become a support, a way of organizing life. This explains why willpower alone is so often not enough — and it lifts the shame. Žižek would remind you that the way out is not to become "perfect" but to find another support, another form around which a life can be built.
addiction.practice: Ask yourself: "What does this circuit give my life — shape, rhythm, shelter?" If you wish, you can talk about it with people who know this path from the inside, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after — with a headache, anxiety, shame and gaps in memory — is hard, and you deserve gentleness, not judgment. Žižek would suggest looking at who exactly is judging you in the morning. Following Lacan, he describes the "superego" — an inner authority that first commands "Enjoy!" and then punishes you for enjoying. The paradox of the superego, for Žižek, is that the more you obey it, the stronger the guilt. From this point of view, one could say that the moral hangover is not the voice of truth about you, but the work of this cruel authority, which can never be satisfied. You don't have to pass sentence on yourself. You can notice the guilt without agreeing with its conclusions, and simply take care of yourself today.
hangover.practice: Write down the loudest accusing thought of this morning, and next to it answer: "This is the voice of the superego, not the final truth about me."

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, and you can enjoy it. Žižek would most likely say something about it that is both joyful and sober. Speaking to protesters in 2011, he said: don't fall in love with yourselves; the carnival comes easily, what matters is what remains the day after, when we have to return to normal life. From this angle, one could say that euphoria is valuable, but the real question is not how to hold on to it but what you can take with you from it. This view doesn't spoil the high — it protects it: you don't demand that it last forever, you let it be what it is. And you know in advance that ordinary life afterwards is not a defeat but a place where you can bring what opened up.
euphoria.practice: Ask yourself: "What from this feeling would I like to take into an ordinary tomorrow?" Write down one thing.

crash.text: A sudden drop after a high can be very hard: the colours drain away, and it seems it will always be like this. This is an understandable state, not your fault. Žižek often talks about "the day after" — the moment after a celebration, a revolution, a big event, when you have to return to ordinary life. For him this is not a defeat but the most interesting part: that is when it becomes clear what has really changed. From this point of view, one could say that the comedown is not a refutation of the high but its second half. Žižek's Lacanian view adds that no enjoyment can last without turning into its opposite. The drop is not proof that the good was a lie. It is simply a time when you are back on the ground and can calmly look at what has stayed with you.
crash.practice: Write: "What of the good that happened is still with me today — even just a little?"

panic.text: Panic is frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it feels as if something irreparable is about to happen. This is a very hard experience, and you are not alone in it. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of "the Real" — what breaks through our familiar picture of the world and can't be put into words. Panic resembles such a breakthrough: meanings and footholds vanish for a moment, and only bare experience remains. From this point of view, one could say that one remedy against the Real is language: naming, returning to the symbolic. Right now, in the middle of the wave, philosophy is not the main thing. The main thing is that the wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Naming the things around you is a simple way to lean on the world again.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor, make your out-breath longer than your in-breath, and name aloud five objects around you — slowly, one at a time.

dread.text: Existential dread — "what is all this for?", the sense of an abyss — is one of the deepest human experiences, and it doesn't make you weaker. Žižek wouldn't comfort you with simple answers, but his view can be unexpectedly supportive. Following Hegel, he holds that at the core of a human being lies negativity — a void, a gap, the absence of ready-made meaning. For Žižek this is not a catastrophe but the condition of freedom: if meaning were given in advance, we would be mere mechanisms. Lacan said that "the big Other does not exist" — there is no authority guaranteeing that everything is right. From this point of view, one could say that the abyss you feel is also a space in which people create meaning themselves, together with others, step by step.
dread.practice: Write down one thing that matters to you today — not "in general", but today in particular. Let that be enough for one day.

fomo.text: The feeling that others are living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very common, and there is nothing shameful in it. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the fantasy of "the enjoyment of the Other": it seems to us that somewhere other people are enjoying life more fully, more deeply, for real, and we are deprived of it. This fantasy is almost always exaggerated — after all, those we envy feel the same way about someone else. From this point of view, one could say that the fear of missing out is not information about where things are actually good but the structure of desire itself. Nobody is in "the place to be". This knowledge frees you: you can stop chasing an imaginary centre of life and notice what is happening here.
fomo.practice: Ask yourself: "Who, in my view, is having the best time right now?" And then: "Who do you think that person envies?"

sleepless.text: Insomnia, and the 3 a.m. thoughts that give you no peace, are exhausting, and it is not your fault. Žižek often recalls a dream analysed by Freud: a father dreams of his child who has burned, and he wakes up to escape what he encountered in the dream. Lacan drew a conclusion from this: sometimes reality is a refuge that protects us from something too heavy. From this point of view, one could say that at night, when the day's tasks and roles recede, what we have been putting off comes closer. Night thoughts seem final, but they are not — they are what awaits calm attention in daylight. You don't have to solve everything now. You can simply admit, "yes, this worries me", and put off the answer until morning.
sleepless.practice: Write on paper what keeps spinning in your head, in one or two sentences, and add: "I'll deal with this in the morning." Then go back to slow breathing.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: a bond collapses, along with the belief that you can rely on another person. This is real pain. Žižek, following Lacan, says that another person is never transparent to us: there is always an abyss in them that we cannot fully know. Žižek calls this opacity the unsettling dimension of "the neighbour". Betrayal is the moment when that abyss suddenly opens. From this point of view, one could say that your pain doesn't mean you were foolish or blind. No one can fully know another; all trust is a wager, not a calculation. Žižek doesn't suggest giving up trust; he suggests acknowledging its fragility. Your capacity to take risks for the sake of closeness is not a mistake — it is what makes love and friendship possible.
betrayal.practice: Write: "What does this betrayal say about the other person — and what does it not say about me at all?"

jealousy.text: Jealousy is agonizing and very human; you don't need to shame yourself for it. Lacan has an expressive pun — jalouissance, a fusion of "jealousy" and "enjoyment" (jouissance). Žižek develops the thought: jealousy is often tied to a fantasy about the enjoyment of the Other — that the rival, or the loved one themselves, is getting something we are deprived of. We suffer not only from what is happening but also from what we fill in ourselves. From this point of view, one could say that jealousy often paints pictures more vivid than reality. That doesn't mean your fear is unfounded — but it helps to tell what you know apart from what you imagine. Making that distinction gives you back a little freedom.
jealousy.practice: Divide a page into two columns: "what I know for sure" and "what I imagine". See which column is longer.

resentment.text: An old grievance is a weight you carry with you, and often there is a real injustice behind it. That deserves acknowledgement. Žižek would ask an unexpected question: could it be that the grievance itself is holding us? From a Lacanian point of view there may be a hidden "enjoyment" in it — jouissance: we replay the scene again and again, and in that painful repetition there is something hard to give up. This is not a reproach, nor a reason for shame — many human feelings work this way. From this point of view, one could say that noticing this circuit is the first step towards freedom from it. Letting go of a grievance doesn't necessarily mean forgiving or excusing; it means reclaiming the energy that goes into repeating the past.
resentment.practice: Notice how many times today you have gone back to this story in your mind. Each time, gently note: "the circuit again" — and shift your attention to what is right in front of you.

heartbreak.text: A broken heart really hurts, and it needs time. When Žižek talks about love, he stresses how radical it is. Falling in love, in his view, is an encounter that knocks us out of our habitual life, an event that cannot be planned. We love not an ideal image but a particular person — with all their imperfections. That is why a breakup destroys not just a relationship but a whole world that grew up around that encounter. From this point of view, one could say that your pain is in proportion to how deeply you were touched. It is not a sign of weakness but the trace of a real event. Žižek doesn't promise quick comfort, but the very capacity to love like this and to lose like this remains yours — it doesn't leave with the other person.
heartbreak.practice: Write one sentence about what this love changed in you — what you learned about yourself and the world because of it.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be found out is familiar to very many people, and it says nothing about your real worth. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "symbolic mandate": a title, a post, a role is something society gives us, not a natural property. A judge is a judge not because there is some judge-essence "inside" him, but because he has been invested with that place. From this point of view, one could say that in a sense everyone is a bit of an "impostor" — there is always a gap between a person and their role. Those who don't feel it are not more genuine; they simply notice the gap less. Your feeling is not an exposure but honesty. You can perform a role without being it entirely.
impostor.practice: Write: "My role is …, and I am more than this role." Notice how the tension changes when you don't have to coincide with it completely.

quote.text: If a man who thinks he is a king is mad, a king who thinks he is a king is no less so.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: "Presentation on Psychical Causality" (Žižek often cites this idea)

self_hatred.text: If your inner voice is merciless towards you, that is very hard, and you deserve gentleness. Its verdicts are not the truth about you. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, explains why this voice is so cruel. The superego — the inner critic — is built paradoxically: the harder we try to please it, the stricter it becomes. Žižek calls this authority "obscene": it is not a fair judge but an insatiable overseer who will never say "enough". From this point of view, one could say that the cruelty of the inner critic is not proof of your guilt but a feature of the mechanism itself. So it is pointless trying to become so good that it falls silent. You can only learn not to take it at its word, and to listen to other voices — fairer and kinder ones.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic and add: "This is the superego talking, and it can never be satisfied. I don't have to agree with it."

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling, especially when it seems nothing can be changed. It deserves compassion. Žižek is known for a provocative piece of advice: sometimes, when everyone demands immediate action, it is better to stop and think. He observed that frantic activity often just sustains what we would like to change. From this point of view, one could say that your powerlessness is not necessarily a defeat. Perhaps it is a pause in which old ways of acting have stopped working and new ones have not yet been found. Žižek also reminds us that "the big Other does not exist": there is no all-seeing authority that has already decided nothing will change. The future is not predetermined, and there is room for hope in that. The first step might be not a leap but a clear question.
helplessness.practice: Put one question on paper: "What exactly can I not change right now — and what might I at least be able to understand?"

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is not laziness or a flaw of character. Žižek, following Lacan, would offer an unusual view. Desire, for Lacan, is sustained by lack: as long as a task hasn't been started, it stays ideal, full of possibilities. Starting means facing an imperfect result, and the fear of that can hold us back. From this point of view, one could say that putting things off protects the dream of flawless execution. Žižek often quotes Beckett: "Try again. Fail again. Fail better." This thought takes the pressure off: nobody expects a perfect start from you. The first step can be clumsy — and that is exactly why it is real. Sometimes it's enough to allow yourself to do it badly in order to start at all.
procrastination.practice: Allow yourself to do the first five minutes of work deliberately "badly" — a rough draft, a sketch, a crooked first line.

uprooted.text: Being torn away from home — emigration, moving, losing the ground under your feet — affects a person deeply, and your sense of loss is legitimate. Žižek, who grew up in Yugoslavia, a country that no longer exists, knows well how a familiar world can vanish. His philosophy offers an unexpected view. Following Hegel and Lacan, he holds that a human being is, in principle, never entirely "at home" — not even in their own culture, not even in themselves. In each of us there is a gap, a foreignness. From this point of view, one could say that emigration makes visible what was always there — and that knowledge can set you free. Žižek also sees a special possibility in the position of someone "not quite one of us": an outside view lets you notice what locals don't see. Your uprootedness is both a loss and a new point of view.
uprooted.practice: Write down one thing you see in your new place because you came from outside — something the locals may not notice.

overload.text: Overload from the flood of news, messages and the endless feed is real exhaustion. You don't have to keep up with everything. Žižek observed that in today's world we are offered endless choice and endless information, but this doesn't make us freer: the more options there are, the heavier the burden of decisions and the stronger the anxiety that we've missed something. Following Lacan, he says that "the big Other does not exist" — there is no authority that knows everything and keeps track of it all. From this point of view, one could say that you don't need to be that all-knowing authority. Nobody knows everything; nobody has read the whole feed. Letting go of complete information is not irresponsibility but an acknowledgement that you are human.
overload.practice: Choose one topic you follow out of habit and allow yourself a week of not knowing any news about it at all.

unreality.text: The sense that everything around you, or you yourself, somehow isn't real can be strange and unsettling. It deserves gentle treatment. Žižek thought a great deal about the nature of reality. Following Lacan, he holds that what we experience as "reality" always rests on an invisible frame — language, habits, the fantasy that gives the world its coherence. In Welcome to the Desert of the Real he discusses how, in The Matrix, the hero discovers that the familiar world was just a picture. From this point of view, one could say that the feeling of unreality can arise when this frame temporarily loosens and the world loses its usual density. That doesn't mean "something is wrong" with you. The frame comes back, especially if you gently lean on simple things and sensations.
unreality.practice: Touch something near you and describe three of its qualities aloud: "cold, smooth, heavy." Words help the world become solid again.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience, and it is worth savouring fully. Žižek, following Kant and Lacan, thought a lot about the sublime. Lacan defined sublimation as raising an object to the dignity of the Thing: an ordinary thing suddenly begins to glow with something greater than itself. Žižek called one of his major books The Sublime Object of Ideology. From this point of view, one could say that awe is a moment when the world briefly goes beyond the familiar and the useful and becomes something inexpressibly large. There is nothing naive about it. It is a reminder that reality is not exhausted by what we know about it. Such an experience doesn't need to be explained right away — you can simply live it.
awe.practice: Stay for one more minute with whatever filled you with awe, and try not to search for words — just look or listen.

relief.text: Relief is a warm and well-earned feeling: something heavy has let go. You can simply enjoy it. Žižek would probably notice something important in relief. Often what weighs on us is not the situation itself but an imagined gaze — that of what Lacan called the "big Other": an all-seeing judge to whom we are constantly accountable. Relief sometimes comes when that gaze weakens for a moment: it turns out that nobody expected the impossible from you, that the catastrophe didn't happen. From this point of view, one could say that relief is a small discovery that "the big Other does not exist". The world is not as strict as we thought. This moment is worth remembering — it may come in handy next time the pressure returns.
relief.practice: Write one sentence: "I was afraid that…, but actually…" — and keep it for the future.

calm.text: Peace and tranquillity are a precious state, and you can simply enjoy them. Žižek is suspicious of calm that becomes an escape from the world: he criticized the fashion for "Western Buddhism", which helps us take part calmly in the frantic race without changing anything in it. But he values a different calm — the one Hegel spoke of when he wrote about "tarrying with the negative". This is not the absence of contradictions but the ability to bear them calmly without demanding final harmony from life. From this point of view, one could say that your calm doesn't have to be perfect or everlasting. It can live alongside the unfinished and the imperfect — and that is exactly why it can be real. You can simply stay in it.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and note what in your life remains unresolved — and that you feel calm all the same.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a lively, joyful feeling, and it's worth greeting with gratitude. Žižek speaks a lot about the "event" — something that arises unexpectedly and changes the frame through which we see the world. Inspiration is like a small event: suddenly something appears that wasn't in the usual patterns. Žižek values such moments, but warns against two traps: expecting complete perfection from an idea, and being afraid of failure. He often quotes Beckett: "Fail again. Fail better." From this point of view, one could say that inspiration doesn't have to become a flawless result straight away. What matters more is that it has opened a new possibility. You can let it unfold without being frightened that the first attempts will be imperfect.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down in its rawest form, without correcting it, and add one small action you could start trying it out with.

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but Žižek would say it reveals a lot about the nature of desire. He loves retelling an old joke. A witch offers a peasant: "I will grant any wish of yours, but I'll do the same to your neighbour twice over." The peasant thinks, then asks to be deprived of something, just so his neighbour gets it twice as bad. The point is that our pleasure, according to Lacan, is often linked not to what we have but to what the other lacks. Žižek sees in this an envy built into desire itself. From this point of view, schadenfreude is not your personal corruption but a universal human mechanism. Once you notice it, you can smile at yourself as at the hero of the joke — and in doing so already slip a little out of its grip.
schadenfreude.practice: When you notice schadenfreude, tell yourself this joke in your head and ask: what do I actually want for myself, rather than against the other?

contempt.text: Contempt gives you a pleasant feeling of purity: I am not like them. Žižek often recalls Hegel's figure of the "beautiful soul" — the one who condemns the corrupt world from on high without noticing that they take part in it and even need it in order to remain its judge. For Žižek this is not an accusation but a description of a trap everyone falls into. From this point of view, one could say that contempt often protects us from an uncomfortable question: what role do I myself play in what I despise? Asking it doesn't mean giving up judgment: you can still consider someone's behaviour unacceptable. But contempt will give way to a clearer, calmer view — without the pedestal, on which it is very lonely to stand.
contempt.practice: Ask yourself: what does the position of the one who despises give me? What feeling might it be protecting me from?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, almost bodily feeling, and it can be directed at people, situations, even yourself. Žižek, following Lacan, observes that what disgusts us is often not the person as such but their "enjoyment" — the way they eat, laugh, live, smell, everything that seems both foreign and too close. Lacan coined a word for this intimate foreignness: "extimacy". Žižek shows that many prejudices are built on this: it seems to us that another's enjoyment threatens our own. From this point of view, disgust says more about us — about our boundaries and fears — than about what caused it. And if it is turned towards yourself, that too is "extimate": everyone has something in them that feels alien, and that is normal.
disgust.practice: Name what exactly disgusts you: the person themselves, or the way they enjoy life? Just note the difference.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and you want the one who hurt you to feel the same. Žižek, drawing on psychoanalysis, writes a great deal about "fantasy" — the inner scene that gives shape to our desire. Revenge fantasies often bring relief precisely as fantasies: in them we regain the power we lacked at the moment of the injury. Žižek stresses that fantasy and action are fundamentally different things, and notes that directly realizing a fantasy usually turns out to be a nightmare, not a satisfaction. From this point of view, the wish for revenge doesn't make you a bad person. You can ask your fantasy: what is the main thing in it — that the offender should hurt, or that it should finally be acknowledged that you were treated unjustly?
revenge.practice: Write down how your revenge fantasy ends. What do you feel at that moment — and where else might you find that feeling?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those close to us is the most shameful kind, because it is aimed at people we love. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, writes a lot about "the neighbour" and observes that the closest person remains at the same time an enigma: there is always something unpredictable and impenetrable in them. Closeness doesn't make the other transparent — on the contrary, it is up close that we run into their incomprehensible desires, habits and demands. From this point of view, one could say that anger at a partner, parent or child is a normal response to this too-intimate encounter with another, not proof of a lack of love. There's no need to unload it on the person you love, but there's no need to consider yourself a monster either. Sometimes a little distance is enough to see the person in your loved one again.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, step out into another room or outside for five minutes. When you come back, ask: what was I expecting from them just now?

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is not a malfunction but, as Žižek would say, the most ordinary structure of a strong attachment. Lacan coined a word for it: hainamoration, fusing the French haine ("hatred") and enamoration ("falling in love"). Žižek shows more than once that wherever we are deeply involved, opposing feelings inevitably arise: the other means so much to us that their imperfection wounds us all the more. He is sceptical of the ideal of "pure" love without contradictions. From this point of view, your ambivalence is a sign of a real bond, not its absence. You don't have to choose which of the feelings is true. Both are true, and admitting that is already a relief.
ambivalence.practice: Say to yourself in one sentence: "I love you — and it irritates me that…". Don't choose between the parts of the sentence.

guilty_relief.text: Relief you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, after someone leaves, even after the death of a seriously ill loved one — often comes together with heavy guilt. Žižek, following Freud and Lacan, explains guilt through the "superego" — an inner authority that, paradoxically, becomes stricter the harder we try to live up to it. You can care for someone for years and still feel you didn't do enough. Žižek stresses that the voice of the superego is not a wise conscience but an insatiable overseer that you don't have to believe. From this point of view, your guilt is this authority at work, not a just verdict. Relief, meanwhile, is the honest response of body and soul to the end of a long strain. Love and relief can live side by side.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down what the voice of guilt is telling you. Then ask: would I say this to a friend in the same situation?

indifference.text: Sometimes something "should" move you, yet you feel nothing — and that is frightening. Žižek offers an unexpected view through the concept of "interpassivity": we often hand our feelings over to someone or something else. The canned laughter in sitcoms laughs for us; in some cultures, at funerals, professional mourners weep in place of the relatives. Žižek sees in this not hypocrisy but a deep feature of being human: feelings don't have to unfold fully "inside" at the right moment. A ritual, a form, a gesture can carry them for us. From this point of view, your indifference doesn't cancel your connection to what is happening. The feeling may come later, differently, at an unexpected moment — or be expressed in an action rather than an experience.
indifference.practice: If the feeling doesn't come, make one small gesture that expresses it — write a word of support, light a candle. That is enough.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and run away — from a job, a city, a role — is familiar to many. Žižek treats fantasies of escape with interest and a touch of irony. He notes that the fantasy of an "elsewhere" where everything will be different often helps us bear the present — and at the same time lets us change nothing in it. Yet he also values the genuine "act" — a deed that changes the very frame of a situation. From this point of view, your wish to escape says that the current frame has become too tight. It matters to understand what exactly you want to leave behind: a place, or the rules you live by. Sometimes the frame can be changed without going anywhere; sometimes a move is needed. You don't have to decide right away — first it is worth hearing what this wish is telling you.
escape.practice: Finish the sentence: "In the place I want to run away to, I wouldn't have to…". Think about which of those rules is acting on you here.

forbidden_attraction.text: Being attracted to someone who is "off-limits" can be unsettling. Žižek often quotes the apostle Paul: "I had not known sin, but by the law." For him this is a key to how desire works: a prohibition doesn't only restrain desire, it partly generates it, making the object especially alluring. Lacan said that our desire is always bound up with the Other: we want what is marked by someone else's gaze, by a prohibition, by inaccessibility. From this point of view, one could say that the strength of your attraction has a lot to do with the "forbiddenness" itself, not only with the person. That's no reason for shame. You can look with curiosity at what in this attraction belongs to the person, and what belongs to the inaccessibility itself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Imagine for a minute that this person has become completely available and "allowed". What happens to the attraction? Just observe.

quote.text: Man's desire is the desire of the Other.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar XI, The Four Fundamental Concepts of Psychoanalysis (Žižek often cites this formula)

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and of being judged can turn a simple meeting into an ordeal. Žižek loves the joke about a man who believed he was a grain of seed. After treatment he understood that he was a man, not a grain — but on going outside he ran back in terror: there's a chicken out there! "I know I'm not a grain," he explains. "But does the chicken know?" Žižek uses this story to show that convincing yourself is not enough, because what troubles us is the imagined "big Other" — what we believe everyone thinks. From this point of view, you can know that you're fine and still be afraid of other people's gaze; that's not stupidity but how the psyche is built. And remember: this all-seeing assessor is a fantasy, and real people are mostly busy with themselves.
social_anxiety.practice: Next time you feel afraid, ask yourself with a smile: "But does the chicken know?" — and notice who is actually looking at you.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is unsettling: you want someone to guarantee that everything will be fine. Žižek speaks about this through a formula he repeats after Lacan: "the big Other does not exist". It means there is no higher authority — not in society, not in history — that knows in advance how everything will turn out and keeps a plan ready. At first glance this is frightening. But for Žižek it is also a liberation: if the future isn't written in advance, there is room in it for the unexpected, for what he calls an "event". From this point of view, uncertainty is not only emptiness but openness. You don't have to fill it with fantasies of the worst. You can admit "I don't know" — and leave room in that not-knowing for good things too.
uncertainty.practice: Write down the worst scenario you fear, and next to it one unexpectedly good one. Note that both are, for now, equally unknown.

waiting.text: Waiting for an answer, a result, news can be more draining than the news itself. Žižek often discusses Kafka's parable "Before the Law": a man waits for years at the door of the Law, not daring to enter, until he learns that this door was meant only for him. Žižek sees here how waiting itself becomes a trap: we grant those we are waiting to hear from enormous power over our lives. From this point of view, one could say that while you wait, it is easy to give all your time to what is being decided behind a closed door. Your agitation is natural — the answer really does matter. But life isn't only on the other side of the door. Part of it is right here, in this hour of waiting, which belongs to you too.
waiting.practice: Write down what you have put off "until the answer comes". Choose one of those things and do it today.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do makes you replay the past again and again. Žižek, drawing on Hegel, talks a lot about "retroactivity": the meaning of an event is determined not at the moment it happens but after the fact — by what happens next. The past, for Žižek, can't be changed factually, but its meaning can. A mistake can retroactively become a turning point, the beginning of something important — depending on what you do next. From this point of view, your regret is not a final verdict. The story in which this mistake happened is not finished yet, and the next chapter can change the meaning of the earlier ones.
regret.practice: Finish the sentence: "A year from now I may remember this as the moment when…". Come up with at least one version.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is one of the strongest feelings there is. Žižek, following Lacan, says that in the person we love we love something elusive — the "objet petit a", that special, unrepeatable something you can't point your finger at but that makes this person the only one. No one else can replace them, because this "something" can't be reduced to qualities you could list. From this point of view, your longing is so strong precisely because what you miss is not "someone" but this very person. It is not a weakness but a sign of genuine attachment. You don't have to drive the longing away. You can let it be — as a testimony to how special this person has become to you.
longing.practice: Try to describe in words that elusive something that exists only in this person. Notice how the words fall short — and that's all right.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — wars, injustice, people's suffering — can be enormous. In Violence, Žižek distinguishes "subjective" violence, which we see in the news, from "objective" violence, built into the way the world is arranged and therefore almost invisible. He notes that the stream of shocking images creates a sense of false urgency: as if you must immediately feel something and do something, with no time to reflect. Žižek suggests something else — to stop and think. From this point of view, your pain is a legitimate response, not a weakness. But you are not obliged to live through every new horror in real time. A step back is not indifference but a way to preserve your strength and clarity so that you can understand what is happening more deeply.
world_pain.practice: Instead of another news feed, read one calm, thoughtful piece about what troubles you, and write down one thought.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: it seems as if someone has spotted something "wrong" in you and passed judgment. Žižek, following Lacan, would remind you that we never fully know what the other wants — and often the other doesn't know either. Lacan marked this eternal question with the Italian "Che vuoi?" — "What do you want?". The other's desire is opaque, so any refusal is not a precise measurement of your worth but the result of a tangled play of someone else's desires, fears and circumstances. From this point of view, rejection speaks of an encounter between two opaque people, not of a flaw in you. The pain of it is real and worth acknowledging. But the conclusion "something is wrong with me" is your interpretation, not a fact.
rejection.practice: Write down how you explained this refusal to yourself. Then come up with two other explanations that have nothing to do with your shortcomings.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is deep, often rooted in childhood, and it deserves gentleness. Žižek, following Lacan, speaks of the "barred Other": the other person is neither all-powerful nor whole; they have their own fears, doubts and lacks. When we fear being left, we unwittingly imagine the other as a confident master of the situation who could walk away at will at any moment. But most often they are afraid too — of not being enough, of being rejected. From this point of view, your fear is not a prophecy but a response to the unavoidable uncertainty of any living bond. Knowing that the other is just as vulnerable, you can speak your fear aloud — and then it stops being a secret that eats away at you from within.
abandonment.practice: Think about it: what might the other person be afraid of in this relationship? Write down at least one guess.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love is a feeling with nowhere to go, and it hurts. Žižek often returns to Lacan's definition of love as the gift of what we do not have. Love, in this view, is not an exchange of values or a deal in which an investment is owed a return. It is the gift of one's own lack, an openness that can never be guaranteed. That is why love is always risky: the other may not respond, and no merits can change that. From this point of view, the lack of a response doesn't make your feeling a mistake or a weakness, and it is no measure of your worth. You dared to do the riskiest thing a human being is capable of. The pain of it is real — but so is your courage.
unrequited.practice: Write yourself one sentence of acknowledgement: "I dared to love without knowing what would happen, and that was brave."

quote.text: Love is giving what you don't have.
quote.author: Jacques Lacan
quote.source: Seminar VIII, Transference (Žižek often cites this formula)

humiliation.text: Humiliation feels as though something very important has been torn off you, and everyone saw it. Žižek, following Lacan, distinguishes a person from their "symbolic mandate" — their role, status, place in others' eyes: manager, specialist, respected member of the family. Humiliation strikes precisely at the mandate — at how you are seen — and that is why it feels like a catastrophe. But Žižek reminds us that we never fully coincide with our role; there is always a gap between a person and their title. From this point of view, what has been hit is your symbolic position, not who you are. A position can be restored or changed, and you are more than any of them. And in that gap your dignity remains.
humiliation.practice: Write down: which of my roles did the humiliation hit? Then — three things about yourself that depend on no role at all.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is rarely about the body alone — someone's gaze is always present in it. Žižek, drawing on Lacan, distinguishes the "ideal ego" — the image of how we would like to look — from the "ego ideal" — the imagined point from which we are judged and whose approval we strive for. Dissatisfaction with the body is often born not from the reflection itself but from looking at ourselves through the eyes of this imagined judge. From this point of view, the question is not only "how do I look" but also "whose eyes am I looking at myself through". That gaze is usually assembled from advertising, other people's words, old remarks. Once you tell it apart from your own, you can loosen its power a little.
body_shame.practice: When you look in the mirror, ask: whose eyes am I looking at myself through right now? Name that gaze — a person, a magazine, a voice.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, it is both frightening and galling, and these feelings are understandable. Žižek, following Lacan, would call illness an intrusion of "the Real" — something that doesn't fit into your usual picture of yourself and the world. Normally we live as if the body were an obedient instrument; illness reminds us that we are not entirely our own masters, and that knowledge hurts. At the same time, Žižek mocks "Western Buddhism" — the fashionable advice to keep your inner calm at any cost. From this point of view, you have the right to be angry, to be afraid, not to cope perfectly. Illness is not a defeat, nor a lesson that has to be learned "correctly". It is an event you can be honest with, without putting on a show of serenity.
illness.practice: Say aloud or write down how you really are right now — without "but I'm holding up" at the end.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good, legitimate feeling. Žižek, criticizing a culture in which "Enjoy!" becomes an order, would note that today even the joy of success is easily poisoned by the demand for more — "it could have been better", "others have more". The superego, for Žižek, is insatiable: the more we do, the more it demands. From this point of view, healthy pride is a small gesture of disobedience to this voice: you allow yourself to say "I did it" without a "but" attached. Žižek values the concrete act — something that really changed something in the world, however little. Your pride is an acknowledgement of such an act. There's no need to hide it or play it down.
pride.practice: Say aloud: "I did it" — and stop at the full stop, without adding "but".

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a quiet and deep feeling. In his essay "Melancholy and the Act", Žižek looks at it soberly and a little critically: he notes that the melancholic treats a lack as a loss — as if what they never fully had was once theirs and was taken away. This subtle trick makes it possible to keep a precious object at least as a lost one. From this point of view, one could say that gentle sadness is a way of staying close to something that always slipped away a little, and there's nothing wrong with that. Žižek would warn against only one thing — turning it into a hiding place from the present. You can live through melancholy without giving up what is possible now.
melancholy.practice: Write down what your sadness is about. Then ask: did I really have this — or is it what I always dreamed of?
